::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- name the components of the **grammar of graphics** and identify them in any ggplot;
- build a plot **layer by layer**, distinguishing **mapping** an aesthetic from **setting** it;
- add fitted lines, **log scales**, labels, facets and coordinate limits correctly;
- change the overall look with **themes** and save a figure with `ggsave()`;
- apply a few principles of **good, accessible graphics**.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## 1. Why a "grammar" of graphics?

Graphs are a key part of every stage of data analysis: we use them to **explore** data (and find errors), to **check** models, and to **communicate** results. A good graph can make a pattern obvious in seconds that would take a table of numbers a page to describe.

Many plotting tools give you a menu of chart *types* ("scatter", "bar", "pie"). **ggplot2** works differently. It is based on Leland Wilkinson's *Grammar of Graphics* (2005): just as sentences are built from nouns, verbs and adjectives, every plot is built from a small set of independent components. Once you know the components, you can build almost any plot — including ones nobody has named.

| Component | Question it answers | ggplot2 function |
|---|---|---|
| **Data** | Which data frame? | `ggplot(data = ...)` |
| **Aesthetics** | Which variables go to which visual property (x, y, colour, size, shape…)? | `aes()` |
| **Geoms** | Which geometric object represents each observation (points, lines, bars…)? | `geom_*()` |
| **Stats** | Is the data transformed before plotting (counts, smoothers, densities)? | `stat_*()`, or inside geoms |
| **Scales** | How are data values translated into positions, colours, sizes? | `scale_*()` |
| **Facets** | Should the data be split into small multiples? | `facet_wrap()`, `facet_grid()` |
| **Coordinates** | In which coordinate system are positions drawn? | `coord_*()` |
| **Theme** | What do the non-data elements (fonts, background, grid) look like? | `theme_*()`, `theme()` |

The general pattern is:

```{r}
#| label: template
#| eval: false
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2)) +
  geom_something() +
  other_components()
```

Components are **added** with `+` (not with the pipe `|>`).

## 2. Building a plot layer by layer

Do heavier penguins have longer flippers? We build the answer one layer at a time.

**Data and aesthetics only** — the canvas and axes are ready, but nothing tells ggplot2 *how* to draw the observations:

```{r}
#| label: fig-layer1
#| fig-cap: "Data and aesthetic mapping only: an empty canvas with axes."
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass))
p
```

**Add a geom** — each penguin becomes a point:

```{r}
#| label: fig-layer2
#| fig-cap: "A scatter plot: one point per penguin."
p + geom_point(na.rm = TRUE)
```

A **scatter plot** shows the relationship between two numeric variables. Here the cloud goes up from left to right: longer flippers go with heavier bodies. (`na.rm = TRUE` simply silences the warning about the `r sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_len))` birds with missing measurements.)

**Map a third variable to colour**:

```{r}
#| label: fig-layer3
#| fig-cap: "The same scatter plot with species mapped to colour."
p + geom_point(aes(colour = species), na.rm = TRUE)
```

The colours reveal structure that was hidden: the large cluster on the right is the Gentoo species. ggplot2 created a **legend** automatically, because a mapping always needs a key. The colours are the colour-blind-safe Okabe–Ito palette, set for the whole course in the setup file.

## 3. Mapping vs setting an aesthetic

This is the most important distinction in ggplot2:

- **Mapping** (inside `aes()`): a visual property *depends on a variable*. `aes(colour = species)` means "colour each point according to its species".
- **Setting** (outside `aes()`): a visual property is *fixed* for all points. `colour = "steelblue"` means "make every point steel blue".

```{r}
#| label: fig-mapping-setting
#| fig-cap: "Left: colour set to a constant outside aes(). Right: the common mistake of putting the constant inside aes()."
#| fig-asp: 0.45
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Setting a constant colour"
#|   - "A constant inside aes()"
#| layout-ncol: 2
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, size = 2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Setting: colour = \"steelblue\"")

ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "steelblue"), na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Mistake: aes(colour = \"steelblue\")")
```

In the second plot, ggplot2 treats `"steelblue"` as a *data value* (a constant variable with one category called "steelblue"), gives it the first colour of the palette and adds a pointless legend. If your colour or legend looks strange, check what is inside `aes()`.

### More aesthetics: shape, size and transparency

```{r}
#| label: fig-aesthetics
#| fig-cap: "Species mapped to both colour and shape (redundant encoding), bill length mapped to size."
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = species, shape = species, size = bill_len),
             alpha = 0.6, na.rm = TRUE)
```

- `shape` works for categorical variables (up to about six categories are readable).
- `size` works for numeric variables, but our eyes compare sizes poorly: use it sparingly.
- `alpha` (transparency, from 0 to 1) is usually **set**, to reveal overlapping points.

Mapping the same variable to colour **and** shape is called *redundant encoding*: the plot stays readable in black and white and for colour-blind readers.

### Where to put `aes()`

Aesthetics given in `ggplot()` are inherited by **all** layers; aesthetics given inside a `geom_*()` apply only to that layer. This matters as soon as you add a second layer.

## 4. Adding a fitted line: `geom_smooth()`

A **smoother** summarises the trend in a scatter plot. With `method = "lm"` it draws the least-squares straight line (the subject of [Simple regression](../09-regression/38-simple-regression.qmd)).

```{r}
#| label: fig-smooth-groups
#| fig-cap: "Because colour is mapped in ggplot(), both layers are split by species: one line per species."
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-smooth-overall
#| fig-cap: "Colour mapped only in the point layer: a single line for all penguins."
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = species), alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "black",
              linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read these plots

- In the first plot `colour = species` is inherited by `geom_smooth()`, which therefore fits **one line per species**. In the second, only the points are coloured and one overall line is fitted.
- The grey band (`se = TRUE`, the default) is a confidence band for the fitted line, not a range where most points fall; you will learn to interpret it in [Confidence intervals](../08-inference/32-confidence-intervals.qmd).
- `linewidth` controls the thickness of lines (`size` is for points and text).
- Without `method`, `geom_smooth()` uses a flexible curve (LOESS for small data), which is useful for spotting non-linear trends.
:::

## 5. Scales: from data to visual properties

Every aesthetic has a **scale** that controls how data values become positions, colours or sizes — and how the axis or legend is labelled. Scale functions are named `scale_<aesthetic>_<type>()`.

### Axis breaks

The `mtcars` data describe 32 cars from 1974. Here we plot fuel economy against the rear axle ratio (`drat`), with the number of gears as a category:

```{r}
#| label: fig-breaks
#| fig-cap: "Custom axis breaks with scale_x_continuous()."
cars_plot <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(drat, mpg, colour = factor(gear))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Rear axle ratio", y = "Miles per gallon", colour = "Gears")

cars_plot +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2.75, 5, by = 0.25))
```

`factor(gear)` turns the number of gears into a category, so that ggplot2 uses distinct colours instead of a continuous colour gradient.

### Log scales

Some variables span several orders of magnitude. The `msleep` data (shipped with ggplot2) give the body weight and brain weight of `r nrow(msleep)` mammals, from a few grams to several tonnes:

```{r}
#| label: fig-log-raw
#| fig-cap: "On linear axes, a few very large animals squeeze all others into the corner."
ggplot(msleep, aes(bodywt, brainwt)) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Body weight (kg)", y = "Brain weight (kg)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-log-scale
#| fig-cap: "The same data with both axes on a log10 scale: the relationship becomes a clear straight line."
ggplot(msleep, aes(bodywt, brainwt)) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Body weight (kg, log scale)", y = "Brain weight (kg, log scale)")
```

On a log scale, **equal distances mean equal ratios**: from 1 to 10 kg is the same distance as from 100 to 1000 kg. Two good reasons to use one:

1. the data are positive and **right-skewed**, spanning several orders of magnitude (incomes, populations, concentrations, body sizes);
2. **relative** (multiplicative) differences matter more than absolute ones.

Prefer `scale_x_log10()` to writing `aes(x = log(bodywt))`: the points are in exactly the same place, but with the scale the axis labels stay in the **original units** (0.01, 1, 100 kg), which readers understand. Log scales cannot show zero or negative values.

## 6. Labels: make the plot self-explanatory

A reader should understand a figure without reading the code. `labs()` sets the title, subtitle, caption, axis titles and legend titles in one place. Labels can also be computed:

```{r}
#| label: fig-labels
#| fig-cap: "A fully labelled plot. The subtitle is computed from the data."
mean_mpg <- mean(mtcars$mpg)

cars_plot +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Cars with a higher axle ratio tend to be more economical",
    subtitle = paste("Mean fuel economy:", round(mean_mpg, 1), "mpg"),
    caption = "Source: mtcars (Motor Trend, 1974)",
    x = "Rear axle ratio (drat)",
    y = "Miles per gallon",
    colour = "Forward gears"
  )
```

`aes(group = 1)` tells `geom_smooth()` to ignore the colour groups and fit a single line. A good title states the **message** of the plot, not just the variables ("A vs B").

## 7. Facets: small multiples

**Facets** split the data into subsets and draw the same plot for each, with shared axes. This is often clearer than putting many colours on one plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-facet-wrap
#| fig-cap: "One panel per island."
#| fig-asp: 0.4
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ island) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species")
```

`facet_grid(rows ~ cols)` crosses two variables:

```{r}
#| label: fig-facet-grid
#| fig-cap: "Rows: sex; columns: species."
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(bill_len, bill_dep)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_grid(sex ~ species) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")
```

Shared axes make comparisons across panels honest. You can free them with `scales = "free"`, but then readers must check the axis of every panel.

## 8. Coordinates: zooming without losing data

To focus on part of a plot there are two very different tools:

- `coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)` **zooms**, like a magnifying glass: all data are still used.
- Scale limits (`xlim()`, `scale_x_continuous(limits = ...)`) **remove** the data outside the limits *before* anything is computed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-zoom
#| fig-cap: "Left: zooming with coord_cartesian() keeps the fitted line computed on all cars. Right: xlim() drops cars outside the window, so the line changes."
#| fig-asp: 0.5
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "coord_cartesian(): zoom"
#|   - "xlim(): data removed"
#| layout-ncol: 2
base <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lb)", y = "Miles per gallon")

base + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2, 4)) + labs(title = "coord_cartesian()")
base + xlim(2, 4) + labs(title = "xlim()")
```

Other coordinate systems: `coord_flip()` swaps x and y, `coord_fixed()` forces one unit on x to be as long as one unit on y, and `coord_polar()` produces circular charts (see [Categorical plots](26-categorical-plots.qmd)).

## 9. Themes

The **theme** controls everything that is not data: background, grid lines, fonts, legend position. This course sets a global theme (`theme_minimal()` with a few tweaks) in its setup file, so you rarely need to touch it. Complete themes replace all theme settings at once:

```{r}
#| label: fig-themes
#| fig-cap: "The same plot with theme_classic() (left) and theme_bw() (right)."
#| fig-asp: 0.6
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "theme_classic()"
#|   - "theme_bw()"
#| layout-ncol: 2
cars_plot + theme_classic() + labs(title = "theme_classic()")
cars_plot + theme_bw() + labs(title = "theme_bw()")
```

Use `theme()` to change individual elements, after any complete theme:

```{r}
#| label: fig-theme-tweak
#| fig-cap: "Fine-tuning single theme elements."
cars_plot +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 0.5))
```

Other built-in themes include `theme_gray()` (the ggplot2 default), `theme_light()`, `theme_dark()` and `theme_void()`.

## 10. Saving a plot

Store the plot in an object and pass it explicitly to `ggsave()` (by default `ggsave()` saves the *last plot displayed*, which is easy to get wrong):

```{r}
#| label: ggsave
#| eval: false
final_plot <- cars_plot + labs(title = "Fuel economy and axle ratio")

ggsave(
  filename = "figures/fuel-economy.png",  # the extension sets the format
  plot = final_plot,
  width = 7, height = 4.5, units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)
```

(The chunk is not run here because it writes a file.) The path is relative to your project folder, never an absolute path. Use `.png` for slides and web pages, and a vector format (`.pdf`, `.svg`) for printed documents and papers: vector graphics stay sharp at any zoom. Fix `width` and `height` so that text has the same size every time you save.

## 11. Principles of good graphics

1. **Show the data.** Prefer plots that show individual observations or full distributions when possible, rather than only a summary.
2. **Maximise the data-ink ratio** (Tufte): every drop of ink should carry information. Remove heavy backgrounds, 3-D effects, redundant legends and decorations.
3. **Use position for the most important comparison.** We judge positions on a common axis far more accurately than colours, areas or angles.
4. **Use colour purposefully and accessibly.** About 1 in 12 men has some form of colour-vision deficiency. Use colour-blind-safe palettes (Okabe–Ito, set by default in this course; `scale_colour_viridis_d()` for many categories), avoid red–green contrasts, and add redundant encodings (shape, labels).
5. **Label everything** with units, and state the message in the title.
6. **Do not distort.** Bars must start at zero; use the same axes across panels you want readers to compare; say when an axis is logarithmic.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Constant inside `aes()`**: `aes(colour = "red")` maps a fake variable — the points are not red and a useless legend appears. Set constants outside `aes()`.
2. **Using `|>` instead of `+`** between ggplot2 layers. The pipe passes data *into* `ggplot()`; layers are added with `+`.
3. **Forgetting `factor()`** for a numeric code (gears, cylinders) used as a category: you get a continuous colour gradient instead of distinct colours.
4. **Zooming with `xlim()`** when you meant to zoom: points outside are removed and fitted lines change. Use `coord_cartesian()`.
5. **`size` for line thickness.** In current ggplot2 use `linewidth` for lines and borders.
6. **Calling `ggsave()` without `plot =`**: it saves whichever plot was displayed last.
:::

## 12. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. In `ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(colour = "blue")`, is colour mapped or set? What about `geom_point(aes(colour = group))`?

The first **sets** colour (all points blue). The second **maps** colour to the variable `group` (one colour per group, with a legend).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Why would you use `scale_y_log10()` rather than `aes(y = log10(income))`?

The points are in the same positions, but the scale keeps axis labels in the original units (e.g., 1,000, 10,000, 100,000), which readers can understand directly.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. You add `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` to a plot with `aes(colour = species)` in `ggplot()`. How many lines do you get, and how do you get just one?

One line per species, because the colour grouping is inherited. Map colour only in `geom_point()`, or add `aes(group = 1)` to `geom_smooth()`.
:::

[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — your first scatter plot.** Using `mtcars`, plot `mpg` (y) against car weight `wt` (x), colouring points by the number of cylinders treated as a category. Add axis labels.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_24_1
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = ______, y = ______, colour = ______)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lb)", y = "Miles per gallon", colour = "Cylinders")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_24_1"}
`x = wt`, `y = mpg`, and `colour = factor(cyl)` so that cylinders are treated as categories.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_24_1"}
```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lb)", y = "Miles per gallon", colour = "Cylinders")
```
Heavier cars travel fewer miles per gallon, and the 8-cylinder cars are the heaviest and least economical.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — debug.** The author wanted orange, semi-transparent points and *no* legend. Fix the code.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_24_2
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep)) |>
  geom_point(aes(colour = "orange", alpha = 0.5))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_24_2"}
There are two bugs: one in how layers are combined, one in where the constant aesthetics are written.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_24_2"}
```r
ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep)) +
  geom_point(colour = "orange", alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE)
```
Layers are added with `+`, not `|>`; and constant aesthetics are *set* outside `aes()`. Inside `aes()` "orange" and 0.5 would be treated as data values, producing default colours and legends.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — facets and fitted lines.** Plot `bill_dep` against `bill_len` for the penguins, with one panel per species and a straight fitted line in each panel. Does the relationship within species go up or down?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_24_3
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(method = ______, formula = y ~ x, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ ______) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_24_3"}
`method = "lm"` and `facet_wrap(~ species)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_24_3"}
```r
ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")
```
Within every species, longer bills are also deeper (the lines go **up**). Try removing the facets and the colour: with all species pooled, the overall line goes **down**! Species is a confounder — the same Simpson's paradox of [Describing two variables](../05-descriptive/23-two-variables.qmd). More on this in [Correlation](27-correlation.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — log scale.** In `msleep`, plot total sleep (`sleep_total`, hours) against body weight (`bodywt`). Put the x axis on a log scale. Describe the relationship.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_24_4
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(msleep, aes(bodywt, sleep_total)) +
  geom_point() +
  ______ +
  labs(x = "Body weight (kg, log scale)", y = "Total sleep (hours per day)")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_24_4"}
Use `scale_x_log10()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_24_4"}
```r
ggplot(msleep, aes(bodywt, sleep_total)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Body weight (kg, log scale)", y = "Total sleep (hours per day)")
```
On the log scale a downward trend becomes visible: larger mammals tend to sleep fewer hours, with a lot of scatter. On a linear scale almost all animals would be squeezed against the y axis.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — a publication-ready figure.** Create a scatter plot of `body_mass` against `flipper_len` with colour *and* shape mapped to species, one fitted line per species without confidence band, a message-style title, a caption with the data source, axis labels with units, the legend on top and `theme_classic()`. Save it as `penguins.png` (7 × 4.5 inches, 300 dpi) and as `penguins.pdf`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
fig <- ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass,
                            colour = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Penguins with longer flippers are heavier, in every species",
       caption = "Source: penguins (Gorman et al., 2014; R datasets)",
       x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)",
       colour = "Species", shape = "Species") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

ggsave("penguins.png", plot = fig, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("penguins.pdf", plot = fig, width = 7, height = 4.5)
```
Mapping colour and shape to the same variable with the same title merges them into a single legend.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Component | Typical code |
|---|---|
| Data + aesthetics | `ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = g))` |
| Scatter plot | `+ geom_point()` |
| Mapping vs setting | `geom_point(aes(colour = g))` vs `geom_point(colour = "blue")` |
| Fitted line | `+ geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE)` |
| Log axis | `+ scale_x_log10()` |
| Axis breaks | `+ scale_x_continuous(breaks = ...)` |
| Labels | `+ labs(title, subtitle, caption, x, y, colour)` |
| Facets | `+ facet_wrap(~ g)`, `+ facet_grid(r ~ c)` |
| Zoom | `+ coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)` |
| Theme | `+ theme_classic()`, `+ theme(legend.position = "top")` |
| Save | `ggsave("file.png", plot = p, width, height, dpi)` |

- Every ggplot is **data + aesthetic mappings + layers**, refined by scales, facets, coordinates and a theme.
- **Map** variables inside `aes()`; **set** constants outside it.
- Use **log scales** for positive, skewed data spanning orders of magnitude; keep labels in original units.
- Zoom with `coord_cartesian()`; scale limits **remove** data.
- Good graphics show the data, label everything and are readable by everyone.
